paths.title: Start Here
paths.blurb: Seven short readings, none longer than an evening, chosen because they need no preparation and pay off immediately. If you have never read any of this, start at the top.

steps.label: Socrates on trial
steps.blurb: A man explains, to the people about to execute him, why he will not stop asking questions. The founding document of the examined life, and startlingly readable.
steps.author: plato

steps.label: Why he stayed
steps.blurb: His friends have bribed the guards; escape is arranged. Socrates argues himself into remaining. Read it right after the Apology.
steps.author: plato

steps.label: An emperor's notebook
steps.blurb: Marcus Aurelius wrote these to himself, never for us. Book II is where the voice arrives: begin the morning by saying to thyself…
steps.author: marcus-aurelius

steps.label: The quarrel that starts it
steps.blurb: Two proud men fight over a prize and the whole war stalls. Butler's prose moves fast; you can read Book I tonight.
steps.author: homer

steps.label: A man talks himself into murder
steps.blurb: The shortest way into Shakespeare: one scene, one soliloquy, and you can hear a mind working against itself.
steps.author: william-shakespeare

steps.label: Lost in the dark wood
steps.blurb: Midway through life, a man finds himself lost. Longfellow's opening canto, with the line numbers that let you cite it forever.
steps.author: dante-alighieri

steps.label: Feared or loved?
steps.blurb: The most quoted chapter in political thought, and shorter than the arguments about it.
steps.author: niccolo-machiavelli
steps.chunkTitle: Chapter XVII: Concerning Cruelty and Clemency, and Whether It Is Better to Be Loved Than Feared

paths.title: Stoicism in Thirty Days
paths.blurb: A month with the two Stoics who wrote to be used rather than admired: Epictetus, a former slave who taught, and Marcus Aurelius, an emperor who took notes. Alternating books, roughly twenty minutes a day. Read a little and stop; that is how these were meant to work.

steps.label: Days 1–5 · What is up to us
steps.blurb: Epictetus opens with the only distinction that matters to him: some things are in our power and some are not. Everything else follows from it.
steps.author: epictetus

steps.label: Days 6–8 · Begin the morning
steps.blurb: Marcus rehearses the day's irritations before they arrive. Notice that he is talking to himself, not to you.
steps.author: marcus-aurelius

steps.label: Days 9–13 · Training
steps.blurb: How to practice when nothing has gone wrong yet, so that you have something to draw on when it does.
steps.author: epictetus

steps.label: Days 14–16 · The retreat within
steps.blurb: The famous passage about retiring into yourself, and the running argument about death that Marcus never finishes.
steps.author: marcus-aurelius

steps.label: Days 17–21 · On freedom
steps.blurb: Epictetus on what a free person actually is, written by someone who had been owned.
steps.author: epictetus

steps.label: Days 22–24 · On other people
steps.blurb: The books where Marcus is hardest on himself about being hard on others.
steps.author: marcus-aurelius

steps.label: Days 25–28 · Living it
steps.blurb: The last book, and the most practical: what the doctrine looks like on an ordinary afternoon.
steps.author: epictetus

steps.label: Days 29–30 · Leaving
steps.blurb: The final book, written near the end of his life on campaign. Read it slowly.
steps.author: marcus-aurelius

paths.title: The Greek Sequence
paths.blurb: Homer to Plato in the order the Greeks themselves would have recognized: the poems everyone knew by heart, then the history that questioned them, then the philosophy that questioned everything. Ten sittings.

steps.label: The wrath of Achilles
steps.blurb: Every Greek in this path grew up on these lines. Start where they started.
steps.author: homer

steps.label: Hector and Andromache
steps.blurb: The war seen from inside a marriage. The scene that makes the Iliad more than a battle poem.
steps.author: homer

steps.label: Priam in the tent
steps.blurb: An old king kisses the hands that killed his son. Nothing in Western literature has surpassed this ending.
steps.author: homer

steps.label: Herodotus asks why
steps.blurb: The first history: gossip, geography, and a serious question about why Greeks and Persians came to blows.
steps.author: herodotus

steps.label: Thucydides answers colder
steps.blurb: A generation later, history without gods. Pericles' funeral oration and the plague that follows it.
steps.author: thucydides

steps.label: Comedy judges tragedy
steps.blurb: Dionysus goes to Hades to bring back a poet, and Aeschylus and Euripides argue about what literature is for. Athens laughing at itself.
steps.author: aristophanes

steps.label: The trial
steps.blurb: Athens puts its most annoying citizen to death. Philosophy's founding scene.
steps.author: plato

steps.label: A dinner about love
steps.blurb: Seven speeches at a drinking party, each wrong in an interesting way, then Socrates.
steps.author: plato

steps.label: The cave
steps.blurb: Prisoners watching shadows on a wall. Read this book alone if you read nothing else of the Republic.
steps.author: plato

steps.label: The last afternoon
steps.blurb: Socrates' final conversation, and his death. The Greek sequence closes where it must.
steps.author: plato
